chapters.title: Day 1 · London — half a mile, and the year the world closed
chapters.hook: Three places in half a mile of London — a 280-metre street that owns the word “suit”, a club that let a man with a small house live in a palace, and the paving stone Britain measures its road distances from — in the one year, 1872, when the planet finished wiring itself shut.

scenes.subtopic: S0 — Cold open: three places, one year
scenes.learning_goal: Know there are three specific places and one specific year in this film; feel handed something, not sold something.

narration.script: One street, three minutes end to end, and the world's word for made-to-measure. A house you could not buy into: you had to be elected. Every road sign in Britain that says LONDON means this spot. Six weeks before this story starts, the last gap in the wire closed. That autumn a novelist bet that the newly wired world could be circled in eighty days.

scenes.title: Savile Row — the whole subject is 280 metres
scenes.subtopic: S1 — Savile Row: 280 metres, and where the trade came from
scenes.learning_goal: Know how short the street is, that the trade clustered here by accident of customers, that its root is uniform, and what fifty hours of hand-sewing costs.

narration.script: This is the whole subject: two hundred and eighty metres, and you can walk it in three minutes. One block behind Regent Street. Built in the seventeen-thirties as ordinary houses. Nobody planned a tailoring street. Nothing about the street is special. The customers were. Tailors were one street west, dressing the gentry, and they followed them in — a trade cluster, the way Silicon Valley is a cluster. The root here is uniform, not fashion: an army cap-maker of 1771, a navy outfitter of 1785. That shoulder was cut for men who had to ride, march, and be recognised at a distance. Every suit starts as chalk on cloth, cut from a paper pattern made for one person. From seven and a half thousand pounds. An apprentice spends two to six years learning one part of the job. Six years before anyone trusts you with trousers.

scenes.title: The word — a myth, a tribunal and a tape measure
scenes.learning_goal: Know where 'bespoke' really comes from, that the Row's origin story is false, that a 2008 ruling took the word away, and that the answer was the 100-yard rule.

narration.script: Where does the word bespoke come from? The word is about fifty years older than the first tailor on this street. The trade tells it differently: cloth spoken for by a customer, right here. The dates say no. In June two thousand and eight the Row took a cheaper rival to the advertising regulator: four-hundred-and-ninety-five-pound suits, machine-sewn abroad, sold as bespoke. The Row lost. Bespoke and made-to-measure, the regulator said, now mean much the same thing. The other pressure is rent. A chain store opened at number three in 2013; in 2016 the council wrote planning protection for tailoring on this street. So they stopped defending the word and defined the thing — by geography: made within a hundred yards of Savile Row. A hundred and sixty-nine firms in 1912. Nineteen by 2006. Twenty-two houses today — and the Row's first woman head cutter in 2009, with her own shop by 2016.

scenes.title: No. 1 — where the journeys were planned
scenes.subtopic: S3 — No. 1 Savile Row: the Royal Geographical Society, and the tailor who bought it
scenes.learning_goal: Know that No. 1 Savile Row was the Royal Geographical Society, that Livingstone lay there in 1874, and that the tailor who bought the building had dressed the explorers who planned their journeys inside it.

narration.script: At the bottom of the street: number one, Savile Row. From 1870 to 1912 this was the Royal Geographical Society: the room where British expeditions to Africa, Asia and the Pole were planned. David Livingstone's body lay here in April 1874, before Westminster Abbey. And on this same two hundred and eighty metres, in a novel published that autumn, a man is packing to go round the world. The premise is an argument, not a character. A newspaper table in the book says eighty days is now possible, and writers had been making that case since Suez opened. A bet, half a fortune, eighty days. In 1912 the military tailor at number one bought the explorers' headquarters for thirty-eight thousand pounds — partly because the firm had dressed so many of the men who planned their journeys inside it.

scenes.title: Clothes, then club — the walk through St James's
scenes.subtopic: S4 — The half-mile walk: why this quarter exists
scenes.learning_goal: Know that the quarter exists because the King moved in, and that the shops along the walk are the court's supply chain.

narration.script: This walk is a Victorian gentleman's supply chain. Fogg walks it every day at half past eleven, counting his steps. Half a mile. Everything in this film happens on it. Henry the Eighth built the palace at the bottom in 1536; it became the monarch's London home when Whitehall burned in 1698. The quarter grew up to serve it. The world's oldest hat shop has been here since 1676. A wine merchant since 1698. A bootmaker since 1866. Every ambassador to Britain is still accredited to the Court of St James's, a palace no monarch has lived in for two centuries. Clothes, then club.

scenes.title: What a London club actually was
scenes.subtopic: S5 — The club as an institution
scenes.learning_goal: Know the club as an institution — a second home with servants, entered by election, in a quarter that held hundreds of them.

narration.script: Three doors in a row on Pall Mall. Three institutions. This is what a club gave you: a man with a modest London address got the run of a palace. Dining room, library, billiards, bedrooms, servants. You could eat, read, write, take your post and sleep, without letting anyone into your own house. You did not apply. You were proposed and seconded, then the membership voted with balls dropped in a box. Black balls kept you out — that is where the word comes from. Churchill resigned from this club in 1913 because a friend was blackballed. At their height there were hundreds of them, packed into a few streets; half the principal ones founded within thirty years. Next door, the Travellers — founded in 1819, in its own words, for gentlemen who had travelled abroad. Your club announced your politics: the Tory club at one end of the street, the reformers' three doors along.

scenes.title: The Reform — a political party built as a palace
scenes.learning_goal: Know that this club was built to fight the one down the road, and that it did the work a party headquarters does now.

narration.script: Budgeted at thirty-seven and a half thousand pounds. It finished at eighty-two. Six floors, three of them below the street — kitchens and the engine that heats the whole house underneath everything. In the eighteen-thirties a club did the work a party headquarters does now: registering voters, whipping, picking candidates. This one opened with a thousand members, nearly two hundred and fifty of them MPs, to counter the Tory club down the road. A celebrity chef in 1837. Alexis Soyer helped design these kitchens, then published them as a book. People came to tour a basement. A members' library of eighty-five thousand volumes, all of it donated — which is why a member needed no study at home.

scenes.subtopic: S7 — The bet, the route and the bank

narration.script: A card table at the Reform, an afternoon in October 1872. A newspaper says eighty days is now possible. One of the players says it lies. Eight legs, and the days land as they go. They add up to eighty. Twenty thousand pounds — half his fortune. Back in this room on the twenty-first of December, a quarter to nine. Eighty days. Nineteen hundred and twenty hours. scenes.title: 1872 — the year the world closed into a circuit
scenes.learning_goal: Know why 1872 was the first year the journey was possible: a port, twelve termini, an underground, an electric street, and a wire that closed round the planet six weeks earlier.

narration.script: Why was 1872 the first year anyone could seriously try this? Because of this: the largest port in the world. Eight hundred thousand tons of cargo a year in 1800; eight million by 1880. Every steamer timetable in the story radiates from here. This film is thirty-one years too late. There is no moving picture of 1872 — this is the Strand in 1903, and it is the closest thing that exists. Close to four million people. A quarter more than Beijing. The river wall he crosses was two years old. In 1878 it became the first street in Britain permanently lit by electricity. Twelve main-line termini by 1865. No other city on earth had anything like that many. The world's first underground railway was nine years old, and carried nine and a half million people in its first year. Between 1870 and 1872 they ran a wire up the middle of Australia — thirty-six thousand poles — to meet the cable from Java. It was finished on the twenty-second of August 1872. From London that October you could telegraph almost anywhere a steamer called. He races the ships. The news about him travels instantly.

scenes.title: Charing Cross — the point London is measured from
scenes.subtopic: S9 — What Charing means, and what stands there
scenes.learning_goal: Know what Charing means, what the twelve crosses were, why the datum is the statue and not the replica, why a station is here, and where half of Brunel's bridge went.

narration.script: This is the middle of London. Officially. When a road sign in Scotland says LONDON, it means this bronze horse. Charing is Old English: cierring, a bend in the road. Not chère reine — the name is a century older than the queen. Eleanor of Castile died in Nottinghamshire in November 1290. Her husband raised a stone cross at every place her body rested on the road to Westminster, so travellers would pray for her. The last night before the Abbey, so the biggest of the twelve. Parliament pulled it down, and the parish sold the stone for paving. That bronze was cast in 1633, ordered destroyed, hidden by the brazier told to melt it, and sold back. It faces where Charles the First was executed. The cross in the station yard is an 1865 replica, two hundred yards off the real spot. Brunel's footbridge came down for the railway bridge. Its chains sold for five thousand pounds, and finished the Clifton Suspension Bridge at Bristol. Why a station here? The company's only London terminus was on the wrong side of the river. This one opened in 1864, eight years old the night Fogg leaves.

scenes.title: A quarter to nine
scenes.subtopic: S10 — The bag, the cab, the rain and the train
scenes.learning_goal: Know what a Bradshaw was, what a hansom was, what the fog really was and what a guinea really was — and that London still has working gas lamps.

narration.script: Almost no luggage — a fifth of his fortune in cash. That red book is a Bradshaw: the world's first compiled railway timetable, 1839, sixpence. By 1872, hundreds of pages of trains and steamers: the internet of the age, in a satchel. A hansom: two wheels, the driver perched behind and above you, a hatch in the roof. Sixpence a mile. He gives her the twenty guineas he won at cards, without breaking stride. Four hundred and twenty shillings: eight hundred miles of cab at sixpence a mile. A sum, not a coin: a price that outlived its own money, and still how Savile Row quotes a suit. Tonight it simply rains. The famous pea-soupers were winter coal-smoke, not weather; the worst killed prize cattle at Smithfield the next year. About thirteen hundred gas lamps still burn in London, tended by lamplighters. Past New Cross the valet remembers the gas burning in his room. It will burn for eighty days, at his master's expense.
